subtype: Panic in a crowded or stressful place [Actor]
passage:
Dear Dolma,
You asked why I was so quiet on the phone on Monday. Here's the truth. On the 8:40 local to Churchgate, pressed between elbows and bags, I suddenly went hot all over. My fingers tingled, my chest locked tight, and every part of me screamed to get off, even though the train was moving. I honestly thought I'd faint.
Then I remembered what you told me after your exam-hall scare: breathe out slowly, hold something solid, and remind yourself it's a wave that rises and falls. So I gripped the metal pole, felt how cold it was, and counted my out-breaths. I told myself, this is the top of the wave. It will go down. By Dadar it had.
I'm going to see a doctor about it, like you did. Thank you for teaching me that.
Gautam

qa.a: Gautam gripped the metal pole.

qa.q: What did Gautam feel on the crowded local?
qa.a: Gautam felt terrified and trapped: hot all over, with tingling fingers, a locked chest and a desperate urge to get off.

qa.q: What helped Gautam ride out the panic until it passed?
qa.a: Slow out-breaths, holding the cold metal pole and remembering that the wave rises and then falls.

qa.q: How might Dolma feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Dolma may feel moved and glad that advice from Dolma's own exam-hall scare helped Gautam through it.

subtype: Panic in a crowded or stressful place [Actor]
passage: So, Tejas, you want the exam-hall story for the episode? Okay. Second-year finals, a hall with two hundred desks and none of the fans working. Ten minutes in, heat started in my neck and spread to my face. My hands tingled so much I dropped my pen. My chest felt like a belt was being tightened, and all I wanted was to run for the door. I'm Nikita, I'm usually the calm one, and I was sure I was about to faint in front of everyone. What saved me was simple. I pressed both palms flat on the wooden desk and felt its grain. I breathed out long and slow. And I kept telling myself, it's a wave, it peaks, then it drops. It peaked. It dropped. I wrote the paper. Afterwards I went to the campus clinic just to check, and they helped me find a counsellor.

qa.a: The hall had two hundred desks.

qa.q: What was Nikita afraid of during the exam?
qa.a: Nikita was frightened of fainting in front of everyone and desperately wanted to run for the door.

qa.q: Which actions helped Nikita stay and write the paper?
qa.a: Pressing both palms on the desk, breathing out long and slow, and remembering that the wave peaks and drops; later came a clinic check and a counsellor.

qa.q: How might other students in the hall have seen Nikita, if they noticed at all?
qa.a: They probably saw only someone pausing with hands flat on a desk, not the storm Nikita felt inside.

passage: Zubin, you asked what happened on the train. It's me, Sarika, and I'm fine now, I promise. It was the eight-fifteen, the ladies' compartment so packed I couldn't lift my arm. Somewhere after Bandra it started. My face went hot, my fingers tingled, and my chest felt squeezed. Every part of me screamed get out, but the next station was minutes away. I wanted to push through everyone. Instead I gripped the cold steel pole with both hands and just felt it. Cold. Solid. I breathed out slowly, like blowing on hot tea. And I told myself what the counsellor said: it's a wave, it peaks, it goes. It kept rising, and I kept breathing. Then, near Dadar, it crested and started to fall. By Churchgate I was just tired. I still take that train.

passage:
Monday: Ten minutes into the economics exam, the hall felt airless. Ishita's hands tingled, her chest tightened and she was sure she'd faint. She asked to leave and sat outside, shaking, the paper half blank.
Wednesday: Her friend Ojas sat with her in the canteen. 'I get it before cricket trials,' he said. 'Press your feet into the floor. Breathe out longer than in. Remind yourself it's a wave, it goes up and comes down.' They practised twice.
The next Friday: In the statistics exam, the heat rose again. Ishita put both palms flat on the cool desk and felt the wood. Breathe out. Wave. Her heart thudded, peaked, and slowly eased. She picked up her pen and finished the paper, a few minutes late but whole.

qa.a: The economics exam.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling on Monday in the hall?
qa.a: She was scared and panicky, sure she would faint, with tingling hands and a tight chest.

qa.q: What did Ishita change by Friday?
qa.a: She pressed her palms on the cool desk, breathed out slowly and reminded herself it was a wave that would pass.

subtype: Panic in a crowded or stressful place [Actor]
passage: Ojas, beta, you're nervous about the Kumbh crowds? Let your Mohit Chacha tell you. I was twenty, travelling home at Diwali, and the Howrah platform was a sea of people. Somebody's bundle pressed into my back, the air smelled of smoke and sweat, and suddenly my whole body went hot. My hands buzzed like bees. My chest felt locked, and one thought filled me: get out, get out. But there was nowhere to go. An old porter saw my face. He put my hand on the iron pillar beside us. 'Hold this. Breathe slow, son. It's big now, it will get smaller.' I held that pillar like it was my mother's hand. I breathed. It grew, it grew, and then it began to shrink. When the train came, I got on.

qa.q: Where was Mohit when the panic started?
qa.a: On the Howrah platform.

qa.q: What was young Mohit feeling on the crowded platform?
qa.a: He felt trapped and panicked, hot all over with buzzing hands and a locked chest, desperate to get out.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Mohit's story?
qa.a: The old porter put his hand on the iron pillar and told him to breathe slowly because the feeling would get smaller.

qa.q: How might the old porter have seen young Mohit?
qa.a: The porter probably recognised a frightened young man and felt kind enough to stop and steady him.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a young adult panicking in a packed crowd and getting through it with slow breathing, something solid to hold and knowing the wave will pass.

subtype: Panic in a crowded or stressful place [Actor]
passage: The Virar fast stopped dead between stations, and the ceiling fans stopped with it. Lavanya, wedged against the door in the ladies' compartment, felt heat flood her face. Her fingers tingled, her chest squeezed, and everything in her screamed get out, but there was nowhere to go. She gripped the cold steel pole and pressed her palm flat against it. Slow breath out, longer than in. She told herself, 'This is a wave. It will peak, and it will pass.' She counted the bolts on the door. Her phone buzzed: Pankaj. 'You ok? Heard trains are stuck.' She typed with one thumb: 'Panicky, but breathing. Passing.' Eight minutes later the train jolted forward, and so did she.

qa.q: What did Lavanya count?
qa.a: The bolts on the door.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling when the train stopped?
qa.a: She felt panic rising: heat, tingling fingers, a squeezing chest and a desperate urge to escape.

qa.q: Which techniques helped Lavanya ride the wave?
qa.a: Pressing her palm on the cold pole, a long slow out-breath, reminding herself the wave would pass, and counting bolts.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt reading 'Panicky, but breathing'?
qa.a: Pankaj was probably worried, but also relieved that Lavanya was coping.
